speaker_role: independent counselor (College Essay Guy staff: former admissions officer/college counselor Susan Tree, plus community manager Tom Campbell, former admissions staffer)
commercial_incentive: College Essay Guy sells counseling/essay services; podcast is promotional content for the brand but the discussion itself is substantive and not a hard sell
key_insights: Selective colleges generally expect four years each of English, math, social studies, science, and a language, embracing the most rigorous options available at a student's specific school
The Common Data Set (C-section) and a college's own admissions website list required and recommended high school coursework; students should check both
Admissions officers use the school profile to see what courses were actually offered, then judge whether a student took advantage of the top available rigor, not an absolute national standard
AP course levels aren't interchangeable in admissions weight; e.g., AP Environmental Science is generally viewed as less rigorous than AP Chemistry, though still valued
If a school offers both AP Language and AP Literature, admissions readers at sub-30%-acceptance schools may wonder why an applicant skipped one

Unusual elective choices (e.g., a niche aquaculture-based biology class instead of AP Bio) can be viewed as a rigor gap unless the applicant explains the reasoning in the Common App additional information section
For IB diploma candidates, readers first check whether the student is a full diploma candidate and which higher-level subjects were chosen relative to intended major
Percentage of a high school's graduates attending four-year colleges (found in the school profile) affects how much 'softness' (B's, A-minuses) in an application admissions may tolerate
specific_numbers_or_facts: IB predicted scores crossing the 40-point threshold (out of 45) are described by Susan Tree as something top US colleges immediately notice
Susan Tree says roughly 95% of colleges/universities publish a Common Data Set on their website, usually under institutional research rather than admissions
notable_or_distinctive: The speaker (a College Essay Guy staffer) gives a candid personal anecdote of choosing a unique aquaculture-themed biology elective over AP Bio and later realizing admissions readers likely saw it as a rigor gap since she didn't explain her reasoning at the time.
reliability_notes: Long, conversational podcast episode from a paid counseling brand; the advice is generally consistent with mainstream admissions guidance but is anecdotal/unofficial (not sourced to any single college's stated policy) and reflects the two speakers' personal experience rather than data.
